title: Schizophrenia: A New Approach
author: Humphry Osmond and John Smythies
summary: Osmond and Smythies propose that schizophrenia involves a naturally occurring adrenaline derivative chemically similar to mescaline, which would account for the overlap between mescaline intoxication and acute schizophrenic episodes.
excerpt: "Mr. Gladstone, with that candour which a great Statesman can afford, once said, 'Government is a rough business, and the results are most unsatisfactory.' ... surely, 'rough business and unsatisfactory results' would not be an unfair summing up?"
citation: Humphry Osmond and John Smythies, "Schizophrenia: A New Approach," Journal of Mental Science 98, no. 411 (April 1952): 309–315.
rights: In copyright (Royal College of Psychiatrists / Cambridge University Press). No US Government interest.

draft.rationale: The theoretical starting point for Osmond's whole psychedelic-research career and for the biochemical (adrenochrome/transmethylation) hypothesis of schizophrenia that dominated one wing of 1950s psychiatric LSD/mescaline research. Written from St George's Hospital, London. This work motivated Osmond's human LSD and mescaline trials and led eventually to his 1957 coining of "psychedelic." A necessary complement to the archive's existing psychoanalysis-and-LSD item, representing the rival psychodynamic wing. It is the founding paper of the adrenochrome research programme pursued at Saskatchewan Hospital through the 1950s.
